evidence: Columbia CUIMC press release title 'Addictive Use of Social Media, Not Total Time, Associated with Youth Mental Health' is a distinctive paraphrase of Xiao 2025 JAMA (paper 3): addictive SM/phone use trajectories (SMAQ/MPIQ) predict suicidal behaviors and mental health, with the key finding that quality (addictive pattern) matters more than total time. Columbia affiliation also consistent with paper 3's Weill Cornell Medicine/NYP affiliation.

Medscape article 'Addictive Screen Use, Not Total Time, Linked to Poor Mental Health in Teens' with snippet 'Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study... addictive use of social media, cell phones' uniquely maps to Xiao 2025 JAMA (paper 3): SMAQ and MPIQ (addictive SM/phone use) trajectories predicting poor mental health in ABCD youth. The 'not total time' framing is a signature finding of paper 3.

Medscape 'Sleep and Social Media Impact Youth Brain Development' (June 2024) with snippet noting shorter sleep duration correlated in ABCD sample. Provisional IDs include paper 177 (Kiss 2023 Health Psychology — COVID pandemic effects on screen time and sleep in ABCD) and paper 314 (Kiss 2026 Journal of Sleep Research — neural sensitivity to SM and sleep; too late for June 2024 publication). Paper 177 is the most plausible match given date alignment. Confidence < 0.7 due to lack of body text; flagged for human review.

Medscape 'Teen Cannabis Use Tied to Slower Cognitive Development' covers ABCD data on cannabis use predicting cognitive development — no corpus paper examines cannabis as the primary IV predicting cognition. Out-of-corpus topic.

Medscape 'Top Predictors of Substance Initiation in Youth Flagged' covers ABCD data on predictors of substance initiation broadly — snippet references 'previous studies examining predictors of substance use initiation in ABCD focused primarily on...' indicating a new predictor study not involving SM/phone use as primary IV. No match to corpus papers.

Medscape 'Motor Abnormalities a Harbinger of Serious Mental Illness?' covers ABCD motor function data in 10,835 children — no corpus paper covers motor function or psychosis as primary outcome. Out-of-corpus topic.
Medscape 'Stimulant Medications Don't Cause Psychosis, New Study Finds' uses ABCD data to study stimulant medication and psychosis — no SM/phone variable involved. Out-of-corpus topic.

Medscape 'Older, Impulsive Teens More Open to Vaping, Smoking' covers ABCD data on susceptibility to e-cigarette and cigarette use based on impulsivity and age — no SM/phone use variable as IV. Out-of-corpus topic.

Medscape 'Can the Developing Brain Weather Climate Change?' models brain imaging parameters after the ABCD Study for climate change neurodevelopment research — no SM/phone variable involved. Out-of-corpus topic.
Medscape 'How Wildfire Smoke May Harm Brain Health' uses ABCD data on wildfire smoke exposure and brain health in 10,000+ youth — no SM/phone use variable. Out-of-corpus topic.

Neuroscience News 'Addictive Screen Use, Not Time, Tied to Teen Suicide Risk' directly and distinctively paraphrases paper 3 (Xiao 2025 JAMA): addictive screen use trajectories (SMAQ/MPIQ) predict suicidal behaviors in ABCD youth, with the key qualifier that addictive pattern (not total time) drives risk. Three-element L3 match: exposure type (addictive screen use), outcome (suicide risk/behaviors), and qualifying finding (not total time).

Neuroscience News 'More Social Media, More Depression: Study Links Cause and Effect' (May 22, 2025) maps to paper 8 (Nagata 2025 JAMA Network Open — social media use and depressive symptoms during early adolescence). The causal language ('links cause and effect') matches paper 8's cross-lagged panel design showing bidirectional but predominant social media → depression path (β=0.07–0.09). Paper 215 (Al-shoaibi 2025 Childhood Obesity) is about BMI/waist circumference, not depression — excluded from match.

Neuroscience News 'Personality Traits and Social Media's Influence on Teen Depression' (Jan 2024) — the personality traits moderator framing is not a primary feature of any corpus paper. Paper 8 (Nagata 2025 JAMA Network Open — SM and depressive symptoms) does not focus on personality traits, and the Jan 2024 publication date predates paper 8 (2025). Likely covers a non-corpus ABCD paper examining personality as a moderator of SM-depression association.

Neuroscience News 'Screen Time in Tweens Predicts ADHD, Slower Brain Growth' (Nov 2025) maps better to paper 435 (Nivins 2025 Pediatrics Open Science — Digital Media, Genetics, and Risk for ADHD Symptoms in Children) than to provisional paper 84 (Shou 2026 Acta Psychologica — putamen volume/cognition). Paper 435 reports social media use (cross-lagged) predicting inattention/ADHD symptoms (β=0.03) with a brain development angle from Karolinska Institute. 'Tweens predict ADHD + slower brain growth' maps to Nivins' combined digital-media × ADHD × neurodevelopmental findings.

Neuroscience News 'Infants Exposed to Excessive Screen Time Show Differences in Brain Function Beyond Eight Years of Age' (Jan 2023) focuses on infant screen time exposure — ABCD Study begins at ages 9-10, not infancy. This article covers a different cohort study (likely Japanese or Canadian infant cohort). Not an ABCD paper.

Neuroscience News 'Screen Time's Link to Autism and ADHD Explored' (Oct 2023) — the autism (ASD) + ADHD + screen time genetics focus does not match any corpus paper. Corpus papers on ADHD (50, 435) are from 2025 and don't emphasize ASD. This likely covers a non-corpus ABCD paper examining screen time and ASD/ADHD genetics predating our included papers.

Neuroscience News 'Video Games Can Boost Children's Intelligence' (May 2022) maps to paper 190 (Sauce 2022 Scientific Reports — digital media impact on children's intelligence controlling for genetics and SES). The finding that video games positively associate with intelligence while controlling for genetic differences is the headline result of Sauce et al. 2022. Date alignment (May 2022) and topic (video games + children's IQ/intelligence + ABCD) satisfy L3: exposure (video game/socializing screen time), outcome (intelligence), sample (ABCD children), effect direction (positive for games).

Neuroscience News 'Children's mental health affected by sleep duration' (Feb 2020) — provisional paper 381 (Zhang 2026 Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychopharmacology — screen time and irritability network analysis) is a 2026 paper, clearly mismatched. No corpus paper from 2019-2020 focuses specifically on sleep duration and children's mental health as primary finding. Likely covers an early ABCD sleep paper outside the corpus.

Mad In America 'The Digital Mental Health Paradox' (May 2026) — the 'paradox' framing aligns with paper 3's (Xiao 2025 JAMA) signature finding that addictive screen use matters more than total time for youth mental health, which is frequently framed as paradoxical. Published well after paper 3 and provisional ID matches. Confidence 0.70 (no body text available); flagged for human review.

Psychiatric Times 'Teen Suicide Attempts Linked to Late Night Screen Use and Medication Access' (Sep 2025) — provisional paper 3 (Xiao 2025 JAMA — addictive screen use trajectories and suicidal behaviors). 'Teen suicide attempts' + 'screen use' aligns with paper 3, but 'late night' and 'medication access' elements are not distinctive features of paper 3. Could potentially also cover a different non-corpus ABCD paper. Confidence < 0.7; flagged for human review.

Psychiatric Times 'Social Media Use in Older Adults May Promote Positive Psychosocial Outcomes' (Jul 2025) — covers older adults, not adolescents. ABCD Study focuses on children ages 9-10 at enrollment. This is a study of a different population entirely; not an ABCD paper.

Psychiatric Times 'Screen Media Activity in Youth: Friend or Fiend?' (Oct 2021) — likely an aggregator review article. Provisional IDs include 388 (Lees 2020 BMC Public Health — screen media activity and displacement of recreational activities, N=9,254 ABCD) and 156 (Hisler 2020 Sleep Health — screen media use and sleep disturbance in children). Both 2020 papers fit the Oct 2021 publication date for a review piece. Papers 136 and 400 (both Zink 2024) are too recent. The 'friend or fiend' framing of a broader ABCD screen time review plausibly cites Lees 2020 and Hisler 2020. Confidence 0.72 given no body text; flagged for human review.

Psychology Today 'Youth mental health concerns are more complicated than just screen time' (Jul 2025) — the 'more complicated than just screen time' framing is a clear paraphrase of paper 3's (Xiao 2025 JAMA) central finding: addictive use patterns, not total screen time, drive youth mental health outcomes. L3 match on two elements: finding (addictive use > total time) and outcome domain (youth mental health).

Psychology Today 'Suicidal behaviors in youths track compulsive social media use' (Jul 2025) directly paraphrases paper 3 (Xiao 2025 JAMA — addictive screen use trajectories and suicidal behaviors). Three L3 elements: exposure (compulsive/addictive social media use), outcome (suicidal behaviors), population (youths). Title is essentially a plain-language restatement of paper 3's main finding.

Psychology Today 'New research offers a clearer answer to the social media and depression link' (Jul 2025) with snippet 'Drawing on data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study — one of the largest long-term studies of adolescent brain and mental health.' ABCD Study named + social media + depression + 'causal clarity' framing maps to paper 8 (Nagata 2025 JAMA Network Open — social media use and depressive symptoms, cross-lagged longitudinal design from UCSF). L4: ABCD Study named + social media topic + configuration consistent with paper 8.
